headline: High risk of prompt-injection and cascading errors: Khoj’s retrieval outputs can feed LangGraph workflows that write and act on unverified content.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Khoj ingests indexed personal notes/files and can use optional web search, so attacker-controlled content can enter its outputs. LangGraph is a library where developers wire nodes/edges, so if its graph consumes Khoj output directly, instruction-like text can be treated as data. The pairwise pathway exists, but no shared channel is documented, so medium is the cautious choice.
conditions: IF LangGraph nodes consume Khoj retrieval text without a provenance filter, injection becomes actionable.
IF Khoj indexes attacker-supplied notes or web content, malicious instructions can propagate into the graph.
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to Khoj outputs before passing them into LangGraph.
Insert a prompt-injection scanner on the handoff step.
Require LangGraph nodes to ignore instruction-like text from retrieval results.
Restrict Khoj indexing to trusted sources only.
requires-engineering: add structured output schemas between the agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Khoj touches personal notes and indexed documents, while LangGraph can write application-defined files and send data to model providers or developer tools. If they share a workspace or checkpointer-backed state, sensitive note content can flow from Khoj into LangGraph outputs or logs. The profiles do not prove a shared filesystem, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or checkpointer store, note content can leak into graph state.
IF LangGraph logs or forwards retrieved text to a model provider, sensitive notes may leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Separate Khoj notes from LangGraph state storage.
Disable logging of raw retrieval payloads in LangGraph.
Review and redact sensitive note fields before handoff.
Use distinct credentials and storage locations for each agent.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data boundaries in the orchestrator.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Khoj can read files and has broad network egress; LangGraph can execute shell, spawn subprocesses, write files, and run browsers. If both are pointed at the same directory or mutable state, they can overwrite or race on shared artifacts. The profiles show overlapping write/read surfaces but not a guaranteed lock, so the conflict is real in default integrations.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory, LangGraph writes can race with Khoj reads.
IF the orchestrator does not provide locking, concurrent updates can corrupt shared artifacts.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Turn on file locking in the orchestrator.
Avoid letting LangGraph write into Khoj-indexed paths.
Schedule non-overlapping runs for the two agents.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency control around shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Khoj produces retrieved answers from personal notes and documents, and LangGraph is explicitly a graph of nodes where developers wire downstream actions. If LangGraph treats Khoj output as authoritative, it can trigger shell, browser, or tool actions on unverified content. That creates a dangerous default pathway with potentially irreversible effects, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF LangGraph routes Khoj output into action-taking nodes without verification, erroneous content can trigger side effects.
IF a downstream node uses browser or shell tools based on Khoj text, the cascade becomes operational.
mitigations: Insert a human approval step before action nodes.
Require citation or schema validation on Khoj outputs.
Limit LangGraph action nodes to read-only mode during testing.
Add a verifier node that cross-checks retrieved facts.
requires-engineering: redesign the graph so retrieval cannot directly trigger actions.

E_compliance.rationale: Khoj is a self-hostable knowledge manager touching personal notes and indexed documents, while LangGraph is a library that can route those same data classes through developer-defined tools and model providers. If personal or regulated notes are processed by LangGraph’s external model calls, retention and residency obligations can diverge. The profiles do not specify certifications, so medium is the safest supported level.
conditions: IF regulated notes are routed from Khoj into LangGraph model-provider calls, residency or retention rules may be violated.
IF the deployment stores prompts or traces in a third-party service, compliance obligations can diverge.
mitigations: Classify note types before routing them into LangGraph.
Disable external model calls for regulated data.
Set retention limits on LangGraph traces and checkpoints.
Keep Khoj self-hosted data in a separate region from model providers.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data residency and retention.
